utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. For the record, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Ostojic. For the Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer who are present. Any preliminaries? None. We still have to go through the tendering of documents process relating to the last witness. Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Thayer and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and to Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. The list that's been distributed has six documents listed, three of which were used to refresh the witness's recollection during his direct testimony and three which were used during his redirect testimony. There is one typographical error. On the last document identified as P02876, that had, in fact, already been assigned a 65 ter number. This was admitted to the Prosecution's 65 ter list of exhibits by the Trial Chamber's December 6, 2006 decision. So the new 65 ter number - actually, it's the old one - but the correct one is P2671. That's the first Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, do you know the number of the report of the first one, negotiations on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Actually, that has no number. It is the first in that series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But as the report was written, it was not numbered. So the first numbered report actually begins with number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second and third one were used by Miletic Defence, and they are minded to tender it separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I noticed that as well. I believe those are being offered by the Miletic team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we entered the courtroom, this morning the Judges were discussing whether it would be a good idea to have the UN documents, in particularly, these documents related to the negotiations Zepa, in its entirety in a binder form. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would welcome that suggestion. We think that would be helpful to the Court. There are 14 of these negotiations on Zepa documents. Clearly, they weren't of significant relevance to this particular witness for me to have even proofed him with each and every one, much less used them during the examination. I don't think it can but help in some respects for the Court to have the full picture, especially as a number of these exhibits were referred to by my friends. I'm not sure if all of the ones which were referred to are being tendered, but I would also renew my offer - and I've had some discussions in the past with some of my friends - to similarly offer the Ukrainian battalion sit-reps which were, as we have seen, pretty much real time reports that were being sent up the chain in terms of the events that they were experiencing during the VRS assault on Zepa. We've heard references to those. I've referred to those in my examination of other witnesses. We certainly saw liberal use of them with respect to Mr. Joseph's testimony. In my redirect, I could have thrown out just as many Ukrainian battalion sit-reps which showed VRS threats on a particular day, specific threats to kill the peacekeepers as well. We -- our position is that they are what they are. The -- I think they would be helpful for the Trial Chamber to read as well, particularly since I imagine that a selection of those will be tendered so the Court has the full picture. We would offer those as well. We can do that separately. But just to sort of expand on your suggestion, Your Honour, I think that would be a good idea. We can very quickly gather those together, and, in fact, I have a packet already together. It's just a matter of copying them and giving them numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No doubt they can be used when General Smith comes later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: They can be used. I'm not sure whether -- I haven't reached that point in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, leaving that. But I'm wondering whether the Defence would have any say to that, that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would imagine that they will be made liberal use of by my friends, as will other UN documents. So we have no objection to having them all come in now as a packet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm looking at Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might say with respect, I think that's a good idea. Could I make one or two observations? I'm a little surprised, notwithstanding Your Honour's comment, at the list that Mr. Thayer has produced because I'm looking at the transcript for Thursday, the 23rd of August. And at page 14165, when he showed the first document to the witness, he actually said, "It's not something we intend to offer." So I was a little surprised by the change of heart. Having said that, as I've already said, with respect, Your Honour's idea is a good one. We couldn't possibly object, certainly those of us who represent General Gvero, to the Court seeing all these documents. I agree with Mr. Thayer that liberal use of certain documents has been made, and the Court might find it useful to see the whole sequence of these documents. That's the stance that I take because to take any other stance would perhaps be seen as unreasonable. Others, of course, may take a different view. I would invite the Ukrainian battalion sit-reps to be either included or to be a separate bundle adduced in a similar fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Anybody else? Mr. Zivanovic? Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just to respond briefly, the -- for example, that first document which I showed Mr. Joseph was not something -- none of those three documents were documents I had intended to offer into evidence to his testimony. His memory faltered. I had to refresh his recollection. I think they should come in. They were referred to. I think they were also referred to, at least some of them, by my friends. In particular, that first document, although I used it to refresh Mr. Joseph's recollection, became very relevant in the specific questioning that he was subject to with respect to the sequence of events on the 20th of July when he was leaving Zepa; that is, the fighting that some of the sit-reps memorialised that occurred in the evening, the early evening hours, starting at 31900 hours to 1930. There was specific questioning with respect to: "Was that the fighting you heard as you were leaving," as distinct from the bombardment that he clearly testified about and which this particular memo talks about him reporting to Mr. Harland. So for both areas of examination, in terms of refreshing his recollection and in terms of corroborating frankly his -- what I thought was very clear testimony as to the sequence of events: Bombardment followed by small arms fire and mortar fire, which were memorialised in some of the documents the UN Ukrainian sit-reps shown to him by my friends. So for both of those purposes that document became relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I sent my list, and I would like to tender two documents used in cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were going to respond to Judge Kwon's -- one moment. Because we haven't cleared the Prosecution list as yet. So any objections to any of the documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender? I think the point raised by you, Mr. Josse, has been dealt with. Any objections? There are none. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, just for the record, I have no objections to any of the other Defence teams' submissions, just to save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So your documents are admitted into evidence, and they will be marked as exhibits accordingly. Now, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, I'd like to tender two documents. That's 1D373 and 1D374 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- that I used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no objections from the Prosecution. Is there any objection from any of the Defence teams? None. They are so admitted. Who else would like to tender documents? Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. We have two documents, and I'm not sure if they are a 65 ter number. The first is a 28 July 1995 report, ERN number R 0123906. The second one is a sit-com report, the 19th of August -- or July 1995, R 0123425. Both were used in the cross-examination of the witness by Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. No objections from the Prosecution. Any objection from any of the Defence teams? None. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've submitted a list. 6D133 through to 6D136 would now be included in the idea that's been advanced by Judge Kwon and Mr. Thayer, so to speak. 6D131 is a different matter, and I'd ask it for that to be admitted. But before I sit down, could I confirm that the Prosecution are going to do the work in relation to the preparation of these bundles? We would be very grateful for that. I know that in as far as the sit-reps are concerned Mr. Thayer has already done that work because he and I have spoken about it some weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll hit the copier this afternoon, Mr. President. We'll have things distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no objections to the tendering of these documents. There are none. They are so admitted. Madam Fauveau? You also had four documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have documents: 5D413, 5D416, 5D417. And at the same time, this is number 5D8272 and 5D491 [as interpreted], which is 5D873. All these are documents originating from the United Nations. And just to correct the last number, this is 5D419.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our preference, Mr. Josse, Ms. Fauveau and others, Mr. Thayer, is that whatever you are tendering now, irrespective of the fact that they could form part of the two binders that we will be receiving, we've decided that these will be tendered separately as they have, and then the binders will become a court documents, an IC documents, rather than a Prosecution or a Defence. Okay? That's just for your information. Does anybody else wish to tender any other documents? I don't think so. We've covered the four of you. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just two quick items. I noticed on the Beara's team's submission that R 0123425 is a three-page document which runs to 3427. This falls somewhat in line Mr. President with what you just said, but that is actually a part of Zepa negotiations 2. It's just been ERNed under a different numerical sequence. It is the draft demilitarisation agreement that was drafted by Mr. Joseph. You'll, actually, see that document under a different ERN under Zepa negotiations 2 when we finally produce it, but I just wanted to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I also would like -- I don't want to doubt your statement, Mr. Meek, but just to make sure, since they are in the transcript, I just want someone to check on the ERN number given by Mr. Meek to make sure that we've got the right documents. The reason is that when Mr. Ostojic was making use of them, we had some problems at the time, which I've not that sure have been sorted out. Okay. So if there is consultation between you, Mr. Meek, Mr. Thayer, and the registrar, between the three of you, you could confirm that these are the two documents that you had in mind. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the second item, Mr. President - I know it's Monday morning so I'll take a shot at it - while we are on the topic of some of these UN-related documents, Mr. Joseph made specific reference in one of his answers to the UN report. And we've heard reference to this large UN report that was done a few years ago. I think -- I know I have used portions of it in some redirect examination. I imagine it's been used in part in some cross-examination. I would also offer that report as a helpful resource to the Court. It's something, I'm sure, my friends will have something to say about, but it is an important document. It's been referred to in a number of places, including the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. It will be referred to by, I presume, Richard Butler in his testimony. It's been furnished -- I can't say off the top of my head whether it's been furnished to General Smith. But, again, it is one of the central documents in the aftermath of the Srebrenica events. And it's 65 ter 528, I'm being told by Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That may be a step too far. For our part, we would like to think about that particular proposal. I'm not sufficiently familiar with that document, to be frank, to make submissions about it now. And I'd ask at least a week for responding to that particular idea, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll give you two weeks, Mr. Josse, during which you will also perhaps think whether being a United Nations report submitted to the Security Council and to the general assembly is something that we can take judicial cognizance of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have two weeks instead of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A brief oral submission in two weeks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No filings, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Music to my ears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So have we finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just in case you don't find it in the transcript, all these documents are being admitted. There are no translation problems. So that's it. Before we admit the next witness, are there any statements that you wish to make? None. So let's bring him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to welcome you. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text has just been handed to you. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you still in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you still use the title of Colonel? It's me that you have to address for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand your question. I am retired, and I'm a Lieutenant-Colonel [as interpreted], a retired Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey will be -- yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there has been an interpretation error. The gentleman is a Colonel-General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel-General. All right. Okay. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. You're going to be asked a few questions by Mr. McCloskey, whom you've met already, and then he will be followed by various Defence teams on cross-examination. You'll get to know who is who in due course. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Could you tell us your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am Bogdan Sladojevic, retired Colonel-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on 12 April 1946 in Bukvik, Gradiska, and I currently reside in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you born in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, but in Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly in Banja Luka and Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us a brief outline of your educational background?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can. I completed elementary school, the secondary school for economics, and the military academy in Belgrade. In 1970, I became the second lieutenant, and I was a platoon commander for two years. After that, I was the commander of a tank squad for two years, then I was the deputy battalion commander for two years, then an armoured battalion commander for four years; and then between 19 -- may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just slow down a little bit for the interpreters. And if you could tell us -- you were just getting into the year and the rank, so we can understand what rank promotions you've had as you get into the higher command positions. We appreciate the outline form. Just a little slower. Thank you. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. Just keep going where you left off. And --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1981 to 1983, I completed the tactics command school in Belgrade. After that, I was a teacher at the military school in Banja Luka for a year. In 1984, I became the regiment commander at the Manjaca firing ground. In 1990, I left for the Sombor garrison as commander of the armoured brigade, and I stayed there until June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what rank were you when you were the commander of the Sombor garrison?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And go ahead and continue from there.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was transferred from Subotica. I became the commander of the 11th Corps of Slavonia and Baranja in the Vukovar garrison, where I stayed until April 1994. Between April 1994 and September, I was at the disposal in the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, and I was in charge of the combat readiness affairs. In September, I was again appointed as the commander of the mechanised brigade in the Sombor garrison. I remained there until July 1995. I believe that on the 6th of July 1995, I was invited to report to the General Staff where they asked me whether I would like to join the army of Republika Srpska. I agreed, and the order to that effect arrived around the 8th of July at the Sombor garrison. I handed over my duties, and I arrived around the 13th in the morning at the garrison in Bijeljina. From there, I was transferred to Han Pijesak, and this is where I spent the night on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get into more detail of that, but can you -- how long did you spend in the Han Pijesak headquarters area before you received your other assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: From the 13th up to the 19th of July, I believe, if that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll get into those six days a bit later, but where did -- where were you assigned on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as the chief of the operations department there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you continue your outline for us, so we can get a full view of your career, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked there until April 1996. In April 1996, the corps was disbanded, and I was again transferred to the Main Staff as the chief of the armoured units and I stayed there until 1997, January. And in January, I received an order to move the Main Staff, i.e., to transform it into the General Staff at the Bijeljina garrison. I was in charge of that. We did that. And until July 1997, I was the chief of the operations and staff sector in the General Staff. In 1997, in September, I went to the school for national defence which I completed in July 1998. Again, I returned to be the chief of the operations and staff sector, and I remained there until 28 February 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of February 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me talk about my ranks: Major, 1993; Lieutenant-Colonel, 1998; Colonel, 1991; General, 1998; and Lieutenant-General, the 2nd January, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the 13th of July, and try to go through it, as best we can, day by day. The most important day for my questioning will be the period around the 16th and 17th and 18th of July, but let's start. You said you were in Bijeljina on the 13th, and you were then taken to the headquarters, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct. First, I arrived at the personnel in Han Pijesak which was located in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how you've -- just how the headquarters was physically set up at that time? And I think you've said before you've described Han Pijesak, you've described Crna Rijeka, you've described the shelter or bunker. If you could describe those areas for us?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can. When I arrived, I was received by General Miletic. He told me that he was the chief of the operations and education administration, and that he was also performing the duties of the Chief of Staff in the Chief of Staff's absence. That's how I understood it. The staff was in the shelter where I was, and the staff consisted of the Chief of Staff, the operations and education administration, the administration for branches, and the general office. This was the inner Main Staff. The other bodies in Han Pijesak, in the hotel, there was the morale guidance sector, the personnel sector, and the administration for plan, development, and finances. Some 500 metres from the shelter, there were two sheds. One contained the security administration and the other the intelligence; and in Vlasenica, there was the rear command post with all of the pertaining bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the Court has been to Crni Rijeka but did not get to this shelter area. Can you describe what you mean by this shelter? Where was it in relation to those others, the buildings that you said that the intel and security were located?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was to the right in a little forest, and let me just explain briefly. There is a tunnel which is about 100 metres long, which used to be an atomic shelter. It contained several rooms: The operations room, two or three offices, a dining-room, an operations centre and the signals centre. And it is very well secured. In front of it, there is a weakened cottage, and there was a bunker there where General Mladic always stayed. To the left, some 150 to 200 metres, there is a [indiscernible] Containing these two sheds. And in those two sheds, there was the intel department and the security department, respectively. The entrance to the shelter had three or four doors that one had to go through in order to come to the operations room and the signals centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What place did you actually meet General Miletic that first time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the operations room, in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what information did you receive from him besides what you've already said?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He told me that I would be the chief of the operations department, either I or Ljubo Obradovic, who was also a colonel at the time. Colonel Obradovic was on sick leave at the time, and the collegium was supposed to consider whether Ljubo would be sent to the operations department at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or whether it would rather be me. He told me what my duties were to be, and he told me that from now -- then on, I would be working in the operations department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Operations department of where?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In his administration, in the operations and education administration, which was the first department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At the Main Staff or at Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. In the operations and education administration of the Main Staff, which is exactly where General Miletic received me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did -- what happened? Did you end up getting that job or did someone else get it, that job with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. When we returned from [indiscernible], from the reconnaissance mission, General Miletic told me that it had been decided that I would be transferred to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as an operations guy, which means that I would be assigned to the operations and education department with the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreters didn't quite get it when you said "we returned from," blank, "the reconnaissance mission." Can you say where you returned from again?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we went to Baljkovica to pursue a reconnaissance order, the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get into that. So on the 13th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. This transfer to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as an operations officer or whatever, was it to be considered a promotion to the post that he had assigned you to before, or was it same level or lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling just the truth. I was still on paper the commander of the brigade in Sombor. It was not my concern where I would be working. I was assigned to that other duty temporarily. All of my administrative assignment was in Sombor. I was paid from the garrison in Sombor. I was just temporarily assigned to work there, and I was still on paper the commander of the 12th Motorised Brigade in Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just on that one small point, can you just give us some idea of the size of the Sombor Brigade as compared to the VRS, just so we get an idea of what you were going from? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Sombor Brigade has the garrisons in Sombor, Kula, Apatin, and Bogujevo. It had about 120 combat vehicles. The numerical strength in peace was about 3.000 men, and in wartime between 5 and 6.000 men. And it covers the entire region of Backa. That would be the long and the short of it. Its area of responsibility is between the Danube and the Tisa rivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, can you tell us, as I take it your first understanding was that you would be working at the Main Staff, what did you do on, if anything, that first day that you arrived there, the 13th, and into the 14th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I understood General Miletic who told me that I would be doing these things, and I would probably be the chief of the operations and education department in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I assumed that it would be the best for me to go there, and I found it only normal that I would be assigned to those duties, because Ljubo had been my predecessor in the other work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly, what time of day was it that you reported to General Miletic in the shelter on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see any other generals from the Main Staff, or any other generals at all, in the area of the shelter or Crni Rijeka that day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone from that area, no, except for General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do that first day on the 13th, after --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the first day, the 13th, I became acquainted, and I think - I can't be sure - that General Miletic told me to prepare a map of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and to study its area of responsibility. I went down to a cellar. I found a map. There was a section missing. I think I added it on the 18th and I copied that zone to myself, and I made my preparations to be in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Apart from that, I was part of the team. I regularly compiled operations reports, until I went to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That was our main task. And it's also important to say that on the 14th or the 15th, a soldier was killed near the water works, about 100 metres away from the shelter; and by night, we went to visit the men and to stand watch with them from the staff command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you given orders to go out to the soldiers who were standing watch to help that situation in some way?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, just around the command in a radius of 50 to 100 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But who told you to go there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a command and then we took turns. All of us from the staff took turns to go, all the lower ranks, apart from the generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But who gave you the order to go take part in this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In what? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've just said that you've gone out and assisted the young soldiers that were guarding the area, but who gave you the order to go out and do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember? We don't want you to speculate. Just give us your best memory?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a list, 18 to 20: Colonel Sladojevic, then Pejic, and so on. There was a roster, actually, stuck to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned that you took part during those few days that you were there in the working on reports. The Trial Chamber has seen reports from the Main Staff to the Presidency. Did you work on those reports?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did on those reports, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, briefly, there was a team. We would meet in the evening, collect all the information from the corps, and draft the report. There was a different team leader every day, and everybody would bring the information pertaining to their service. It would take us about an hour to compose the report, then we would type it out and take it to General Miletic for his signature; but, first, we would collect all the reports from the corps and from the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you collected those reports from the corps and the subordinate units in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when would you present them to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It would start at about 4.00 p.m. and go on up to around 1900 hours, by code. When one code was processed, it would arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time of -- would you present this to General Miletic for his signature?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Around 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it would be sent off to the Presidency when?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It would be encrypted right away, typed out, and then sent out to all the units and the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to look at some of those reports from the 16th to about, I believe, the 22nd in my office?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you notice your initials on any of them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember which ones?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think the 19th, 22nd, 23rd, but I can explain. There could be an error, because the persons working on encryption would not change the initials. So there might be an error, but most likely it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, if -- from your chronology, you thought you left for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the 19th, but you saw some initials?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I could be wrong, but I'm convinced I went on the 19th; however, if you look at those codes and everything, it turns out it was the 23rd. But to the best of my recollection, the images I have in my memory, I think it was the 19th. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. All right. Now, after you -- you remember being on or going out and assisting the young soldiers on guard duty, what do you remember on the days of the 15th, 16th, 17th? What else, if anything?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th, and the 16th, everything was normal. I didn't see anything else. I have to say that as for the operations in Srebrenica, and so on, I didn't have any information about that in the staff. I didn't deal with that, except for what arrived through the commands and the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And one late afternoon or evening, did you receive information that there -- you would be going somewhere the next day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Trkulja hinted something, but I got the actual order in the morning at around 7.30. I was to take a rifle. We didn't have weapons. I went and was issued with a rifle, and then he said we were going to the Zvornik area. He got a Puh car and we went. That was on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You said you got the actual order from Trkulja on the morning of -- at 7.30?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the hints that -- you said you got hints before that. When did you get the hints from General Trkulja that there would be something?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, there was talk that something had happened in the Zvornik area, but I think the information arrived from the Supreme Command, not from the Drina Corps. I can't be sure, however. It was just a rumour. We didn't see any papers or documents confirming that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a little more information, if you have it, on what was the problem that was rumoured to have happened, or what information did you get?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: We got information that a column of Muslims had been allowed through on the Udrc-Crni Vrh axis towards Tuzla, and that they had passed through the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, who received the order to go to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I got it orally. As for Colonel Trkulja, I don't know whether he received it orally or in writing, but he didn't show me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did Trkulja get it from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Most probably from General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us last time that it was General Miletic that gave him the order?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us last time that you were present when General Miletic gave Mr. Trkulja the order to go to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. I said that he gave him a piece of paper. I didn't see what was written on the piece of paper, nor did Trkulja show it to me. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Who gave Trkulja a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: General Miletic gave him that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That was on the 17th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you hear General Miletic say to Mr. Trkulja?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear. They were saying something, but I can't be sure what. I don't want to speak about things I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did, well, Colonel Trkulja tell you about the orders?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: When we were in the Puh, he said, "It's like a hunting party. There was a kind of stampede in the Zvornik Brigade." I didn't say anything, and then we arrived in the Baljkovica area. And he said that General Miletic had hinted that something was going to happen in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did he say that General Miletic hinted at?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He, Trkulja, said that he had given General Miletic a hint that something would happen in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And had Colonel Trkulja told you that he had been in an area the previous day, on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. But when I was preparing for this trial, from the information of The Hague Tribunal, I got that Cerovic had spoken to Colonel Beara, that Colonel Trkulja would come to the command post of the Drina Corps, and solve the problem of some prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Whether he went to the Vlasenica area on that day or not, I don't know. But according to the documents, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you about documents or what you just referred to about Colonel Beara - that's the first I've heard of that - and what you have learned from evidence that may or may not have been at this trial. I'm not asking you about. I'm just asking you did Colonel Trkulja tell you he had gone somewhere before, on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he didn't tell me where. He just told me he'd been somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he say that he'd been out in the field? I think that's the word you used last time you told us about this.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. He'd been out in the field, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Colonel Trkulja told you that he'd been out in the field on the 16th. Do you know what -- what part of the field do you think he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything about that, but he didn't say he had been in that area where we were. But whether he had been or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then tell us who left from Crni Rijeka? You, Colonel Trkulja. Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: When we got to Baljkovica, Colonel Stankovic was waiting there in full combat gear, and Trkulja told me that Colonel Stankovic would come to the Baljkovica area and wait for us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So Colonel Stankovic was part of the original order to go to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who is Colonel Stankovic, or who was he at the time? Can you tell us what position he had?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood him to be a clerk in the intelligence administration of the Main Staff, the first officer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Desk officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I got that -- well, I concluded that because I know that before that, Colonel Stankovic was in Doboj, and he arrived in the Main Staff; and by the way he behaved, I saw Stankovic at Baljkovica then, and never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So did you have a driver, you and Colonel Trkulja, when you drove from Crni Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. We didn't have a driver. Colonel Trkulja was driving the Puh himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you stop along the way to Zvornik, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the way to Zvornik, we stopped in the command of the Drina Corps. Colonel Trkulja stopped the Puh some 20 metres in front of the command. I remained in the Puh, and Trkulja went into the command of the Drina Corps. He opened the door, went in, into the operations room. He spoke to the duty officer. I don't know who was on duty. All I know is that he was there for ten minutes, maybe less. He came back, and he said, "There is no one here who can give us detailed information about the Zvornik Brigade. Let's go to the Baljkovica area."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the reason you stopped by the Zvornik -- excuse me, the Drina Corps in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably Colonel Trkulja wanted to get some information. He didn't want to go without having the proper information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did he get any information at all, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. He just said that most probably Colonel Lazic would come there, that he had been appointed by the command to monitor or control the Zvornik Brigade. And Colonel Lazic arrived about half an hour or an hour after we did, to the Baljkovica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Lazic, for everyone?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Lazic was the chief of the operations department in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as you know, where did you or Colonel Trkulja receive the information to go to Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Trkulja probably got this information from General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But was -- were you talking about going to Baljkovica before you reached the Vlasenica headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is it possible that the information came from the Vlasenica headquarters to go to Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was expanded in the Drina Corps when we got to the command. I don't think it was clear to us where we were supposed to be going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Baljkovica is a big area, and I think there is Donja Baljkovica and Gornja Baljkovica. Where did you decide to go?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: We decided to go to the command post of the Zvornik Brigade, which was on the slope overlooking the village of Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What kind of command post was this? Was it a temporary forward command post? Did it look like the command post of a battalion, or could it have been a brigade forward command post? You know these command posts better than I do. What kind was it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was there for only a short time, but I can say that it was the command post of a battalion, but that the brigade commander, Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, and two other commanding officers were there with him at that command post. That was the first time I had seen Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. It was at that command post. He was coming with Stankovic. We said, "Hello." That was the command post. It was probably at battalion level, the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that, who you saw and everything, but we'll try to go question by question. It won't take us long. Can you describe: Were you able to drive right to this command post, or did you have to get directions from anyone?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: There is a good road leading up to it. We got there directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And about, roughly, what time did you get there? What time of day? I know exact times are impossible, but, roughly, what time did you get there on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let me go back a bit. Can you tell us what was your understanding of why you were going there with Trkulja to meet Stankovic? What was your purpose, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it was to let the column of Muslims go along the Udrc-Crni Vhr-Tuzla axis to let them through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you there to see anything about why they were allowed to go through?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was someone in trouble for letting them go through, with the Main Staff, as far as you knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Colonel Stankovic. He was, because he was in full combat gear and he asked Vinko whether there were any indicia that the Muslims were about to attack Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may have been a translation issue. Was anyone in the Zvornik Brigade potentially in trouble for allowing the Muslims to go through, with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think the Chief of Staff could be held responsible, and Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did your trip to the Zvornik area have anything to do with going to determine that situation, to see if someone should be held accountable for that, letting the Muslims through?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And tell us who you saw and what you learned, what you did, pursuant to those orders. You started doing that.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I found Colonel Stankovic there. Vinko Pandurevic reported to him and Trkulja. He briefed them. And I concluded that the first wave had gone through fighting, and that there had been enormous casualties. After that, the corridor was opened up, and the remainder passed through without any fighting. That was my conclusion, and Colonel Trkulja accepted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had told us you'd learned that numbers of killed at that day. Do you remember the numbers that you learned that day, of Serb soldiers killed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- well, first, I concluded that they were exaggerating the numbers, but it was approximately correct. The Chief of Staff was afraid we would be taking some measures because they had let the column through. When I was questioned by the investigators, I wrote down there were 49 killed and about 120 out of combat. And this information was not checked because two or three operative reports from the Zvornik Brigade arrived in the Drina Corps, and then from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff, saying that there were a lot of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned the Chief of Staff. Who are you referring to in that statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Obrenovic. He was the Chief of Staff. I knew him from before the war because I was his teacher in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you learn -- did you get information from Obrenovic when you were there at that command post near Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We got information. He arrived later, and he said, "In town, there are major protests. Quite a few people have been killed. There will be problems with the brigades." That's what he told Vinko Pandurevic and Colonel Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was he referring to, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was referring to the men killed and wounded from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear descriptions of the terrible fighting from Commander Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you hear that -- similar descriptions from Chief of Staff Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I? Vinko reported what had happened on the 16th, and I think the last wave went through on the 17th in the morning, up to about 800 hours. And from his description of the events, I understood that in the first wave, there had been heavy fighting; and in the second wave, he probably opened up a corridor and they all went through in the direction of Tuzla. I concluded that the Muslim artillery had not been precise in its targeting and that they had inflicted major losses on their own forces, because there was unprotected manpower out in the open. And Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic explained that there had been three self-propelled guns and that these Muslims had captured some of those, and that they had fired on both our forces and their own forces but from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were there on the 17th, do you recall if that corridor was still open, or do you know, when you were there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, everything was calm. Vinko arrived from the left-hand side. He was talking to somebody on Motorola, and he told Colonel Stankovic that he was establishing contact with the Muslim side in order to deal with the problem of casualties, and I no longer saw the column passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you seen the column passing through in front of your eyes before that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have a place from which to see it, since we had come from below the hill side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The translation I got is that after there was a talking on a Motorola, that you no longer saw the column passing through. Did you ever, while you were there, see the column of Muslims passing through the area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What else do you remember occurring while you're with these officers at the command post?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that Colonel Lazic arrived maybe half an hour later, and that Colonel Trkulja showed a lot of attitude towards him. He was arrogant, and he was questioning him about being late arriving at the command post. We did not talk about the column, about the front line. Lazic and Trkulja were only discussing, while he was in the chief of the Drina Corps, why it was Colonel Andric who was give than duty. The discussion went on; and, finally, Trkulja, to shrug him off, told him, "If you continue, you will not be even what you are now."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So I take it Lazic was angry that Andric got the Chief of Staff job to replace General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have asked you this, but can you describe what Colonel Trkulja's position was at the time and rank?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a retired colonel, and he volunteered in the army of Republika Srpska. The law allowed him to do that. He had arrived from Leskovac, and he was the chief of the armoured and mechanised units with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me of that. All right. And how long did you stay in the Baljkovica area that day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: A long time. Maybe 15 or 16 hours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not correct whether she heard full 15 or 16 hours or up to 1500 or 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sladojevic can you repeat how many hours you think you were there? The reason is that the interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be sure, but I believe that I stayed there between 1100 and 1600 hours; that is, the end of the time I spent. And we worked effectively from 11.00 and 1300 hours, and from 1300 hours on was the time when the two were discussing those issues that I have explained to you. In other words, half of the time we worked effectively, and the other time of the time was spent in that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when did you -- about what time did you leave that command post area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Stankovic left the command post first. He didn't say where he was going. Trkulja and Lazic were still discussing matters. From that place, we went to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Who did?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Trkulja and I. Stankovic did not go with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time did you and Trkulja leave from the command post at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime between 1500 and 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you went to the Drina Corps command, and what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: We had lunch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Then Colonel Trkulja and I went to inspect the units in Konjevic Polje, in the place called Kasaba. Some of the troops of the 65 Protection Motorised troops were there. Those were young soldiers. He spoke to a lieutenant there for a while, and then we inspected the ambushes that had been set up in two or three places on the roads leading from the forests to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you spend the night in Vlasenica that night?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Then we went to the rear command post in Vlasenica. It was already late at the time. We had dinner there, and we spent that night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you go look at the troops in Nova Kasaba and other places before you spent the night or the next day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the following day, we looked at the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So on the 17th, you went to Vlasenica, spent the night; and on the 18th, you looked at the troops?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, in the morning, Trkulja said that we should go and see what was going on on the main road between Vlasenica and Konjevic Polje, and further on towards Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did do you that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: We did. We did that. We inspected the whole road. We did not make any detours. We arrived in Srebrenica. We turned around in a square. And we returned to the points where there were soldiers. We spent sometime talking to them, some of them. We passed through without talking to anybody. We stopped by a Praga. We spoke to the soldiers there, and then Colonel Trkulja said, "Okay, let's go to the Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: We arrived at the Main Staff, at the shelter, sometime between 12.00 and 1.00 or maybe 11.00 and 1.00. I can't remember when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's 1.00 p.m. in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1300 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you or Trkulja report to anyone?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: None of us did. I believe that he reported orally to General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He went to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the shelter?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the shelter, yes. There were two officers in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you go with him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Trkulja tell you what he had told -- what he reported to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Never. There was not much to tell, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you and Colonel Trkulja agree on the judgement of Vinko Pandurevic, or did you have differing views on his actions relating to the column?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say, while we were on the way to Baljkovica, we had a wrong opinion. But when we arrived in Baljkovica, and when I explained to him in professional terms, we agreed on our common opinion. And we said that the situation should be conveyed as it was, and we were of the opinion that no measures should have been taken against the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just explain why you think that Pandurevic's actions were correct and that nothing, no measures, should be taken against him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Pandurevic had taken the right steps. In the first part, he engaged in fighting; and then when he estimated, as the commander, that he would suffer losses, the most realistic and logical thing was for him to open the corridor up and to let the army go through, which is what he did, and it is a good thing that he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any other battles in the Bosnian war where Serbs lost about 49 people in such a short time period?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such situation. I didn't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm almost finished but maybe ten minutes left, but it might be a good time to teak a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break as from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, we left off, it was the day of the 18th, and you've said that Colonel Trkulja had gone to General Miletic's office in the bunker or the shelter, as you've called it. That day, or the next day, that is, either the 18th or the 19th, were you called upon by anyone to discuss your views about the situation that you'd seen in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it was shortly after that, you thought it was around the 19th, that you actually left and took up your position at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'm going to show you a document now. I know you've seen this before. It's number 65 ter 927. It will come up on your screen and in the original B/C/S text. And I'll bring it up so hopefully you can read it, and we see that it's entitled-- that it's from the Main Staff, dated 17 July?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that, in paragraph 1, it talks about the three colonels that you've spoken of: Trkulja, Stankovic and yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as you look at this, had you seen this written order prior to being sent to Zvornik on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw this order two days prior to my first interview in October 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the first time you saw the order was a couple of days before speaking to Mr. Ruez. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you -- who showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Usually, there were preparations either -- by the Ministry of Defence prior to any interview. I was invited to come to the Ministry of Defence, and this was given to me by Cvetkovic, who was the main legal officer at the Ministry of Defence. And he was the one who prepared us for our interviews with The Hague Tribunal, and this occurred in an office or a room at the Ministry of Defence. At the same time, as I was leaving, Colonel Jeserovic [as interpreted] showed it to me and said, "This will be used in your preparations, and this will be used when they interview you." I received this paper at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me clear up the record. Didn't quite get the names. The legal officer that you spoke about, can you repeat his name for us?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Cvetkovic. He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was the one who prepared us, who briefed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Colonel you spoke to, you said, as you were leaving, what Colonel was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: As I was coming to the preparations, Colonel Jeserovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just try to see if it's correct, is it Colonel Keserovic with a K?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: K, K, K, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clear this up, who actually gave you the 17 July document, which one of these people, if --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Keserovic showed it to me, and then Cvetkovic actually gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did -- is the Keserovic -- the Colonel Keserovic that gave it to you, do you know if that's the Colonel Keserovic that's mentioned in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He's on the same list as me, and he was at the same type of preparations a day before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what Colonel Keserovic's position was in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the military police, the 1st Krajina Corps. I don't know exactly, but this is what I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And he is -- he's the same person in paragraph 3, and he received an assignment according to this order.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Having to do with the Bratunac-Milici area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Try to let me finish; otherwise, it will be very hard to translate what we are saying. All right. So did you have any involvement with Keserovic and this description of items in number 3 of this order?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, as we read this order - and I won't go through and read it all - but the first two paragraphs appear to be involved in what your assignment was, particularly the first, of course. It says basically: "Assist in joining of the VRS and MUP forces, planning and coordination combat operation, to block, crush, and destroy lagging Muslim forces." It doesn't say anything about checking up on Vinko Pandurevic and seeing if he's -- seeing why he let the column through. Can you explain the language of this order? How do we -- how do we know that this is the order related to what your job was?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood the assignment given to me by Trkluja as applying only to Baljkovica. I never assumed that it said planning, organisation of combat activities. I believe that the three of us did not even have the strength or the means to pursue this matter or to carry out this order. If we were to carry this order out, we should have gone to the 1st Zvornik Brigade to coordinate with them, which we didn't do, and I believe that nothing contained in the second passage was ever done in respect of carrying this order out, and I claim this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your interview of 2002, you and Mr. Ruez discussed this order a bit. Mr. Ruez --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- mentioned that he had received this through the Ministry of Defence of the RS, and you told him --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- at the time, that one of the generals had given it to the Ministry of Defence. Who did you tell Mr. Ruez had given this order to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said to the general that it must have been General Miletic, but I was wrong. This document was at the Ministry of Defence, and the Minister of Defence at the time was Colonel Mane Milovanovic, who sent it to The Hague Tribunal. I did not like the fact that he had sent it to the Tribunal because only 10 per cent of the things contained in this order were ever carried out; whereas, so many other things which were more pertinent, more relevant, more dangerous, have never been sent to The Hague Tribunal. That's why I asked him who had sent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did -- yesterday in my office, did you clear that up and tell me that it was a mistake what you told Mr. Ruez, and that you meant Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you tell me about one other mistake -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked to see who was it who sent it, and I came by the information that it was Mane Milovanovic who had sent it to the Tribunal. All I was interested in was the truth, nothing else. I wanted to get to the bottom of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also mentioned that General Miletic had some sort of access to the archives of the Main Staff, to Mr. Ruez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I said that I assumed he had access to the archives, but on a second thought I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can you explain why it is that you told Mr. Ruez that he had access to the archives and now you think you're mistaken?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Because I could never establish that for a fact. I assumed that this order had arrived from Belgrade rather than from the Ministry of Defence. Only when I established for a fact that it arrived from the Ministry of Defence did I change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, thank you very much, and I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Now, let's confirm the time you need for the respective cross-examinations. Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I need just five minutes, Your Honour. I have actually just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Mr. Meek, you had asked for 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I had asked for 30. I don't believe I won't use that. I may not use any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Nikolic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Stojanovic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honour. I won't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau, you had asked for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that it will be rather half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, ma'am. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Less than ten minutes, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Haynes, you asked for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Fifteen or 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Who is going first? Mr. Zivanovic, could you please introduce yourself to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Zoran Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel for Vujadin Popovic. I have only one question for you. You said here, and that's on page 19, line 14 and 15. You spoke about an event when you arrived in Han Pijesak - and this was on the 14th or the 15th of July - that a soldier was killed. I wanted to ask you whether you knew about the circumstances of that soldier's death: Who killed him, how?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was killed near the water tank which supplies the Main Staff, I think, probably at around 1.00 at night. He was a young soldier. Most probably, he was killed by people pulling out from Srebrenica or Zepa, and then we strengthened the security and regularly checked on the young soldiers. And it's true that the soldier was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: Do you know at that time there were such events generally?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say so. I can't tell you the precise dates and places and times, but I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Miletic. You mentioned General Mane Milovanovic. He was the Chief of Staff of the army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You come from -- you came to Bosnia from Serbia on the 13th of July 1995. When you arrived in the army of Republika Srpska, you knew that General Milovanovic was the Chief of Staff. Were you aware of that at the time? And after spending a few days in the Main Staff, you went to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: While you were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, you knew that General Milovanovic was the chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Nobody could take that duty over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you arrived in the Main Staff, in the shelter, where you received by General Miletic, could you tell us who was in the shelter at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was only General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down please, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it possible that not a single aide was there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
