utterances.text: There was no one there except the Chief of Staff. All the others had posts further away, by position and by function.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So, even in a normal situation, when General Milovanovic was in the staff of the VRS, only General Milovanovic was in the bunker as regards persons able to command the Army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is no foundation for his knowledge regarding that question. He was only there for six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can only speculate, I think, where General Milovanovic would have been. Proceed with your next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have not received -- one moment, General, please. We haven't on record the interpretation of your question, so if you could kindly repeat it again, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when you arrived on the 13th of July at the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, General Miletic introduced himself to you as the chief of the operations and training of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself as the chief of the administration for education and operations, which is a more general and broader term.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have the information that General Miletic had replaced General Milovanovic in the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When did you learn that General Miletic had assumed the position of General Milovanovic in the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this never happened. He could not have taken over and he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I show the witness Exhibit number 4D -- 5D430. 5D430.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you have just told us that your initials can be found on this combat report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This was drafted on the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness the last page of this combat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I would like to know, particularly, is not your initials because you've already told us this might be a mistake. Actually, it is the name of General Miletic that I'm interested in. It is in -- indicated here as "representing the head of the General Staff" [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain to the Honourable Chamber. General Miletic should have had an order for that. Two orders should precede any standing in for somebody. The first one, 90 days prior to the order coming to -- into the effect, and it is issued by the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I just -- the booth translation was in a tough spot. But if they could look at the English, and they may not have the English translation. But the title that is referred to has been officially called "standing in for the Chief of Staff," and they were struggling with representing Main Staff, something to that degree. And I think it's an important enough issue that we should get that translation correct, that it's "standing in for the Main Staff" is how that document has -- is referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, in replacement of the words "as representing the head of General Staff"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. Do you agree to that? It's a question of translation basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a lot of problems with the interpretation. But the witness has been following the document in B/C/S; and as long as he understands what this is all about, this is what matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's refer the witness back to the document, which is still visible. Can you explain to us, General, the meaning of the words at the bottom of that document: "Zastupa nacelnika staba, General-Major Radivoje Miletic." What does that mean to you as a military officer, with experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. For this, there should be an order: The first one from the superior officer, and this should have been drafted by the commander of the Main Staff, which was General Mladic at the time. And this order can be in effect for no longer than 90 [Realtime transcript read in error "19"] days, and this order should contain this: Who he is standing in for, for how long, and into which payment bracket would that position fall. As far as I know, General Miletic, by position, was in the sixth salary bracket. In order to be performing these duties, he should have been reassigned to the third salary bracket. The salary in this case is very important because the salary carries certain obligations with it. If his position continues after 90 days, then this assignment should be preceded by an order signed by the president of the republic at the salary bracket continues applying and all the benefits with it. When this period expires, he has to be appointed to that position permanently, or rather, somebody else has to take up that position permanently. In other words, nobody can stand in for the chief of the Main Staff after that period. In this case, the Chief of Staff is the Chief of Staff of the whole army, not of only one command post. And I believe that there was no need for this person standing in for the Chief of Staff and signing his orders. He could have performed his duties because he was the most senior officer in the staff, but it was not legal for him to stand in for the Chief of Staff and to sign his orders for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a question just to have these things clear in my mind. Many a time we have come across documents here signed by an individual who is not exactly the person who is sending the letter. And in those cases, before the signature, and before the name who is actually -- should be actually sending the letter, there are the words "Za."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Za: That is according to the law. But his full name has to be typed, and he can use the word "Za" only if he is legally entitled to stand in for somebody. For example, it could read that I drafted a document and that it was signed on my behalf by my deputy, who is entitled to do so by the establishment position and by the salary bracket. He can sign on my behalf when I'm not there. In this case, the case of General Miletic, the only thing we know about him was that he was a chief, and he did not have any other functions or positions, and his duty could only be to perform his job and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Sorry. I just have one additional question, as well, for you sir. In your previous answer, when you were describing the nature of the order signed as standing in for, you indicated at page 48, line 5, "And this order can be in effect for no longer than 19 days?" Is that a correct number? 19 seems an odd number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first order is in effect 90 days or a bit more maybe, and the second order is also in effect for 90 days. And the number was 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you have just told us that General Miletic was only a chief, and he did not have any other positions or functions. When you say that he was only a chief, you meant the administration for training and operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, yes, administration for training and operations. That's what he was chief -- the chief of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that when General Milovanovic was not physically present in the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that there is a problem with the interpretation. In B/C/S, there are two different words describing the General Staff, the Main Staff; whereas, in the French language, there is just one word, and I believe that all the confusion arises from that. I really don't know how to talk to the witness if we are going to be ending up with this confusion between the different terms that apply to different bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to you, Madam Fauveau, in B/C/S, which is -- which one is the correct translation of "Main Staff"?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Main Staff. And I'm talking about one part of the Main Staff, and I believe it could be translated as the staff of the Main Staff, which is the same thing in B/C/S which is the staff of the Main Staff. In French, this does not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So my suggestion is now that the interpreters, both the English and the French ones and the Serbo-Croat ones, have heard what you have to say, if we could kindly use that word only, unless there is an indication that it's another word -- the other word that needs to be used. We would appreciate that. It would simplify matters. Okay. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to -- I'm going to try and clarify and explain the difference with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when we are talking about the staff of the Main Staff, we are talking about one part of the Main Staff, which does not comprise the entire Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that the Main Staff consisted of only two persons at the same time, which was Tito and Mladic. In all the other formations of the world, in all the other armies of the world, there is the General Staff and the Main Staff. This particular staff that we are talking about, where General Miletic belonged to, is actually the fourth part of the General Staff, approximately, by the positions and the number of people in it. According to the salary brackets and establishments, it may be one-third of the General Staff, and it is more better represented in the logistics or the rear sector than the General Staff by the positions and by the number of people in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Miletic was not physically present -- when General Milovanovic was not physically present at the staff of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, General Miletic could replace him in certain duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He could perform some of his duties, but he could not sign documents on his behalf. He could not sign them directly or as preceded by the word "Za," standing in for. Neither of the two is allowed by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When we are talking about certain activities that General Miletic could perform, which would normally be within the purview of General Milovanovic, is it correct that these activities were strictly limited to the activities performed within the Main Staff by the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army. And this time I mean the staff of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same objection. I don't think six days makes him an expert enough to answer that question. I don't think there has been a foundation for that. This is a VJ officer that went and worked for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We think that the -- your submission, Mr. McCloskey, relating to the mere six days of his stay there, is important but it is not of absolute importance. It can be of relative importance, and it can be outweighed by the knowledge obtained by the witness from other sources either prior, then, or afterwards. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and that's all my objection is. He may have gained the knowledge afterward, but if we could just have a little foundation so that these questions make more sense. I don't need him to go into all of it - I don't think any of us do - before a question like that, because there is more information out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now, General Sladojevic, we appreciate, of course, that you were there for a short time. But if you are in a position to answer Madam Fauveau's question, please do so within your best abilities. I will repeat the question to you myself. Madam Fauveau asked you the following: "When we are talking about certain activities that General Miletic could perform, which would normally be within the purview of General Milovanovic, is it correct that these activities were strictly limited to activities performed within the Main Staff, by the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army. And this time I mean the staff of the Main Staff." Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My problem with that is if it's a general -- pardon me, if it's a general question, I think he can answer that. But this is asked talking about the specific situation of General Miletic and Milovanovic which went on for a long time, and he doesn't know anything about except for those six days. So as a general question, can a person in this position do this, I don't have a problem with that. But when he's being referred specifically to this situation and these individuals, I don't think there has been any foundation to establish that he knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we'll see whether he knows it or not, because he may know it or he may not know it. If he doesn't know it, he's going to tell us that. If he knows it, we will expect an answer from him. Yes, General. You still remember my question, or rather, Madam Fauveau's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the question, and I believe that you're all right. As far as I know, from confidential sources, General Miletic could only issue orders to let UNPROFOR columns through, so that they wouldn't wait, and some other auxiliary things and things that didn't really matter that much. He did not have any authority to sign any other orders or issue any other orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you. Madam Fauveau, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before that, if I could just clarify with you, sir. You say at page 54, lines 1 and 2, "as far as I know from confidential sources." What sources are you speaking about in rendering that statement, sir? When you make reference in your answer to "confidential sources," who are you speaking about? What sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember -- it was about UNPROFOR? The last question, my last answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Your last answer, sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a document indicated that General Miletic was entitled to let those column through. I may have misspoken when I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that there is an interpretation error. And in order to avoid any confusion or controversies with the Prosecutor, it is on page 54, line 2. You said that General Miletic could issue certain orders that concerned UNPROFOR, but there is again a mistake. I didn't say that he could issue orders, but that he could carry out orders.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Those were approvals. I -- this would be internal documents which did not matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, General Miletic could not himself decide on the contents of those documents. He could only draft, put into writing something that somebody else had decided already?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a standard form document that went on being copied again and again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you the first page of the document 5D430.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have that document already. I just want to show the witness its first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you see this document was sent to the president of the Republika Srpska and also to the forward command post of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says, "IKM 2," which is exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And General Milovanovic, according to the information that you had at the time, during the time when you were at the Main Staff and the Sarajevo Corps, was posted to this forward command post?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of that command post, and he was also supposed to send reports signed by commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic. He was at the same level with the different corps. He was subordinated to the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is some confusion here. Perhaps you can help us, Madam Fauveau and Witness. The question was: "And General Milovanovic, according to the information you had at the time, during the time you were at the Main Staff," so we are referring to that specific time and Sarajevo Corps" was posted to this forward command post." And then your answer is: "Yes. He was the commander of that command post, and he was also supposed to send reports signed by commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic. He was at the same level with the different corps. He was subordinated to the chief of the Main Staff." What do you mean "he was also supposed to send reports signed by commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic"? We are talking of the same person, obviously, here. So are you suggesting that as commander of that command post, it was his responsibility and his duty to send out reports signed by him? Is this what you're stating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain. When a command post is established, an order is drafted by the commander of the Main Staff. This order appoints the commander, the composition, the command post location, and logistical support. Usually, he is responsible for one area, for one region, and that zone covers an area equalling the area of responsibility of one corps. He receives reports from all of the subordinated commanders; in other words, everybody in the area is subordinated to him. This means that he receives reports from his subordinated officers, the same evening he compiles his own reports and sends it to the Main Staff. And the Main Staff sends him information similar to the information that you see on the screen, and this is what we call an exchange of information in keeping with the law. This is provided for by the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction in the transcript that has led to this confusion. On page 55, line 21, the witness said that he reports to the commander of the Main Staff; whereas, in the transcript, it says the chief of the Main Staff, hence the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when you arrived at the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, General Miletic could not decide that you would be transferred to the Sarajevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't him. He told me that it would be the collegium who would decide that, and the collegium is composed of the commander of the Main Staff, the chief of the Main Staff, and all the assistants. General Miletic was a supplementary member of the collegium who would sometimes attend its meetings, sometimes not; and when he did attend, he was in charge of taking the minutes of the meetings; again, in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You're talking about the security service and the guards around the shelter. Was it something normal, these guards and the security that was provided around the shelter?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the war that is normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Miletic himself did not decide on that. He just drafted an order naming those who would be standing guard duty during certain periods of time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, it was General Mladic who issued a decision, which was supposed to be implemented by General Miletic. It was a war zone, the situation was dangerous, and it was only normal to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In other words, General Miletic was only in a position to write orders and other documents according to the instructions received from the General commander of the army or the chief of the General or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They decided to cut me off apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. It's not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There we go. That is a direct misstatement of his previous question. He said Mladic issued orders and Miletic implemented orders, not that Miletic just wrote issued orders. She can't state it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was also a distinction made between drafting and issuing the orders. But anyway, let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Fauveau, I think the witness himself is in agreement with Mr. McCloskey as you could confirm. So perhaps you could either rephrase your question or proceed with another question. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a very straightforward question: General Miletic was not in a position to make decisions. Can we say that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. He was not in that position. He did not make any decisions, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you need to consult --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, a minute or half a minute even, maybe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we won't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Defence of General Gvero, I will put a few questions to you. Answering the Prosecutor's questions, you said that you did not see any of the high-ranking officers in the Main Staff in those days?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not the Main Staff, but the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That leads me to conclude you did not see General Gvero there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the six days you were there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw him in 1996, I think, in late May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, please, General and Mr. Krgovic. Since you speak the same language, if you could kindly allow a short pause between question and answer, to help the interpreters catch up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Referring to the location where the various administrations of the Main Staff were, you said that the one for morale headed by General Gvero was in the hotel in Han Pijesak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Baljkovica - and this follows from your proofing notes with the Prosecutor - you said that the Main Staff was not informed of what had happened in Baljkovica and Srebrenica at that point in time, before you went out on the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, just, good morning, Mr. Bogdanovic. As you know, I ask questions on behalf of Vinko Pandurevic -- Sladojevic, I'm sorry. Sorry for getting your name wrong. Can we just clarify the position so far as your visit to the forward command post on the 17th of July is concerned. You originally went to Han Pijesak with Colonel Trkluja; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: From Han Pijesak to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. But when you received the order at the command of the Main Staff, it was Colonel Trkluja who went to receive the order, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And then he and you drove from Han Pijesak to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: First to Vlasenica and then to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, during the course of that journey, did Colonel Trkluja tell you what orders he had received?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, orally. We talked in the Puh, and I concluded that we should take measures in the Zvornik Brigade to find out why it had been so easy for that column to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You very nearly answered my next question. Before you arrived in Zvornik, did you understand that the commander of the Zvornik Brigade had opened a corridor to allow the column to pass through, or was that something you did not know at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: The information was not correct. We only assumed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that the commander of the Main Staff was aware that a corridor had been opened on the morning of the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like you, therefore, please, to have a look at a document. It's P1195. And I hope I've got this right. I think A is the English and B is the Croatian -- the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm told that it is confidential document, an intercept, so no broadcast, please. We haven't broadcast any part of it as yet, have we? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The document on the screen in B/C/S is not the correct document. The one on the English channel is the correct document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this correct now? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you would just take the time to read that through to yourself, Mr. Sladojevic, and see how much of that corresponds with your understanding of what you knew on the 17th of July. I'm going to help you with what this is because I don't think you'll have seen anything like this before. This is a transcript of an intercepted radio communication said to be between General Mladic and the Main Staff duty officer at 4.15 in the afternoon of the 16th of July. Tell me when you've read it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was it your understanding that Vinko Pandurevic had, on the 16th of July, arranged passage for the Muslims over the territory of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see this document in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. But what I want to know is what you were told. Were you told on the morning of the 17th, when you were given your orders at the command of the Main Staff, that they knew that Pandurevic had arranged passage over the territory of the Zvornik Brigade, or were you not told that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was not told that. Trkluja and I only assumed it. If this had been on the 16th or the 17th in the morning, probably a much larger group would have gone out on the ground. I think this information was only being checked. That's my opinion. It was not certain at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you know that the source of the information was the President of Republika Srpska himself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I learned that only in 2004. Before that, I never knew it or heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you know on the 17th of July that Pandurevic had been out of communication for a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't remember having that information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you talked to us earlier on about the possibility that you would have to take measures. Did you understand on the 17th of July that if you discovered Vinko Pandurevic had allowed a column to pass, that that would have been in the terms of this intercept unauthorised or without authorisation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand the question. I think that the passage lasted longer, as I was able to understand, from the 16th in the morning, until the 17th in the morning. The first wave that came along, in fact, fared worst, because Vinko at that time accepted combat. The Muslim artillery, which was firing on unprotected columns, inflicted great losses on their own forces. Afterwards, when they captured those three self-propelled guns and started inflicting losses on the Serbs also, I think that Vinko quickly withdrew and let the column pass until the morning of the 17th. That's what I discovered on the spot. When Trkluja and I were on our way, we had one opinion as to what measures should be taken against Vinko, the Chief of Staff; but when we arrived there and found out what had happened, we changed our minds and we then decided that no measures should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think this is something you said in one of your interviews that the measures that you were considering was the immediate removal of Vinko Pandurevic from command, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what you say when you're talking among yourselves, that's one thing, but what you can actually do is quite another. It wasn't up to us to replace him. All we could do was see what the situation was and propose to the commander of the Main Staff what measures should be taken, but it wasn't up to us to decide on the measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So, when you eventually met Vinko Pandurevic and Dragan Obrenovic, they were in the position of trying to defend what they had done by allowing the column of Muslims to pass. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Obrenovic was a bit frightened. He thought disciplinary measures would be taken. Vinko was a true commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it was from Obrenovic that you got the figures of those who were dead and wounded?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard that he repeated that. There were great problems in the town of Zvornik because of the losses and the wounded. Obrenovic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But, importantly, it was he who gave you the figures that you wrote down when you went for your first interview in 2000?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we wrote it down on a notepad very carefully. And I included that information when I was interviewed in 2000, and I noted that down in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was your belief, or it is your belief, that the figures that Obrenovic gave you were exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, to have a look at another document. It's P334.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like the witness to see paragraph 3, please, which I think is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Sladojevic, just take a few moments to read that over to yourself. Have you read it, Mr. Sladojevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Having looked at that, would you agree that it seems very much that Dragan Obrenovic did exaggerate any figures he gave to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the date here is the 27th of March. How he gathered that information, it should be determined precisely. Up there, the 24th and 25th Infantry Division of the 2nd Corps doesn't give a date when did they sustain these losses, and then all these operations have these losses. So it turns out that half of those were in Baljkovica alone. I don't believe there were so many.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much anyway. Can we move on, please. Prior to the 17th of July of 1995, you'd never met Vinko Pandurevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Only those four hours in Baljkovica; and then never again until January, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In 1997, was the army of Republika Srpska reformed so that the Main Staff became the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. In January 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you take an office in the command of the newly formed General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I became chief of the operations staff sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And Vinko Pandurevic also, did he hold an office in the newly formed General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. At that time, there was an ordinance appointing him assistant for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as part of the reorganisation, was the command of the General Staff moved to a different location from that where the command of the Main Staff had been?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Part of the Main Staff who remained working, who did not retire, were moved from Han Pijesak to Bijeljina, and they were appointed according to the new establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did this require the removal of records from Han Pijesak to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But let me add: The order on the reforming and moving of the Main Staff was written by General Miletic, and I was appointed to implement all this and I made the new establishment. I moved everything that had to be moved to Bijeljina, and the new General Staff started operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened when you tried to remove the records from Han Pijesak to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in early February, I was supposed to go to Han Pijesak with three vehicles to take over the documentation. I remember it was snowing, and Vinko Pandurevic, Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, went with me. We arrived in Han Pijesak. We found General Miletic there. He had prepared all those documents to hand them over to us, but he said, first, go to see General Mladic. Vinko went to see General Mladic. He returned ten or 15 minutes later, and said, "Sladojevic, there is nothing doing." We went back to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know what General Mladic said to Pandurevic when he asked if the records could be taken away?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about the records. He saw off Vinko Pandurevic, and he said, "You have many wall nuts in your pockets." And he showed him two walnuts in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Help us as to what that means: "You have many walnuts in your pockets."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The two of them know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was Vinko Pandurevic's relationship like with General Mladic after July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: In Serbian, we use an expression: "Podozrivo," mistrustful, not at a very high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If I may interrupt you a little bit, Mr. Haynes. When you met -- when you arrived in Han Pijesak and you met with General Miletic, and he told you that the documents were ready but you first had to go and see General Mladic, did General Miletic indicate whether it was the two of you that had to go to General Mladic or whether it was one of you and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Only Colonel Pandurevic went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But why was it that Colonel Pandurevic went and not you instead, or why didn't you go with him if the relationship --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was more important than I was in the General Staff. There was no need for me to go also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I just want to see if I can jog your memory. The phrase about walnuts, does that have something to do with somebody doing something bad?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's a very hard question to answer. If I were to say the precise truth, it's 50/50. That means he didn't do what the other one wanted. He sometimes did things on his own initiative, in his own way, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in 1998, I think, you were at a military school together with Vinko Pandurevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1997 and 1998, for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about the course you were both doing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was normal teaching. Vinko was the best in the class. But five or six days before the final exam, a criminal report arrived from the army of Republika Srpska. I still don't know what this was about. A day before the exam, he was banned from taking the exam, and so he did not complete the school. And this criminal document was sent by the late General Momir Talic. I know that for a fact, because they had heard that he was the best in the school; and according to certain systems, they did not find him suitable, so that Vinko did not graduate with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As vague as the walnut story. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd just like quickly, if we can, to go back to P334.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You will see, if you look at the beginning of paragraph 3, the period for which the numbers of dead are described there, and it concerns all operations in Srebrenica and Zepa against the 24th and the 25th Division. So does that help you with the date period that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the date here. Is the date at the top of the document? I don't see when this was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not a date. It just describes events that those dead result from, and it is the operations in Srebrenica and Zepa and the combats against the 24th and 25th Divisions and the 2nd Corps. Do you know when those combats took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you show the date of this report to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. If he can look at the first page, he can see that it is a combat report dated the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So it was up to that date.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult now to determine whether this is in order, because I don't know whether they entered the losses in the column or the losses of the regular army. As far as I can see, the losses refer to the 24th and the 25th Infantry Division. If the division had those losses, it's a pretty poor division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Sladojevic, it's a combat report from the Zvornik Brigade relating to its own losses. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the Zvornik Brigade. No, there is something wrong here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, if you could address the witness straight to the third line of paragraph 3 and ask him to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it's translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I would like is for him to read it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under number 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, third line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In combat operations with the Muslim forces in Srebrenica, Zepa and the remaining parts, and the forces of the 24th and 25th Infantry Division of the 2nd Infantry Corps of the so-called army of BH, the Zvornik Brigade suffered the following losses: Killed, 27; seriously injured, 24; slightly injured ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these losses refer to the losses sustained by the Zvornik Brigade; wouldn't you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I agree, but it doesn't give the time. It's not precise. You have to ask questions precisely, you know. That's important. It should be written here from the 15th of July to, and so on. If this is the same day, then it refers to Baljkovica, but I still don't believe it's the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Haynes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sladojevic, I'll take your advice on board in due course, but I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there any re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to put it now or do you want to put it after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just, this should be very short, if I could do it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Though famous last words, but this really should be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To see if this refreshes your recollection regarding what this criminal problem that Vinko Pandurevic had, did you hear of a problem he had related to some financial matter and an apartment he had in Zvornik? Was that what this was about, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was a surprise. We thought he would be top of the class, but then two days later a criminal report arrived and nobody ever said why. I can draw up as many criminal reports as you like in Republika Srpska. It can have to do with an apartment, a car, whatever. I think it was pointless. If it had not been pointless, it would not have been dismissed by the court. Whatever is dismissed by a court is was pointless and shouldn't have been done. The purpose of that criminal report was to prevent him from graduating and from coming to the Main Staff. I am sure of that, and that is true. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you tell us today that this criminal report had nothing to do with war crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not. I have to be quite honest about that. No. Vinko Pandurevic, in 1998, had no idea there were criminal proceedings against him. He would certainly have come, just as everybody else did: Krstic, Talic and everybody else. He have done the same. But the main problem was that they wanted to prevent him from graduating and coming to the territory of Republika Srpska where Talic and the others were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have any further questions for you, General Sladojevic, which means you're free to go. You will be assisted by our staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for having come over to give testimony, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McCloskey, is the next witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I had estimated a little bit longer, as you could see. We, also on the request of the Nikolic team, not to put this on them, but we switched two witnesses and that cost us a delay of about a day, but with the estimates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then do you have any practical suggestions as to how we could utilise the third session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to get the issue of the Pandurevic statement to Eileen Galleece sorted out, and I was hoping that we would have had something accomplished on that. Perhaps I could speak to Mr. Haynes at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I had made arrangements to talk to Mr. Vanderpuye now. I said after this witness we would talk about it and we would resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's do this. Let's have a break now, and then we go through the documents, if there are documents that you wish to tender in relation to this last witness, and see whether we can do anything useful during the third session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Documents, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just had that one 17 July document, 65 ter 927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objections? None. Admitted. Madam Fauveau, would you like to tender any documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any other Defence teams, I suppose not, from following the cross-examination? Okay. So that concludes the testimony of General Sladojevic. Now, you have confirmed to us that the next witness, Mr. Lazarevic, although he has arrived this morning, he's not ready to testify today also because of the switching of witnesses and that you agreed upon with some Defence team at the 11th hour. That is understandable. But if there is a way in which we could utilise the time we have left, we are here precisely for that. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's just a testament that to this is being run very well, this case. We don't have anything to talk about, unless, I think, Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. Haynes were still discussing that issue we spoke of earlier. But we couldn't come up with anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I see Mr. Haynes is blissfully silent about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We've made an appointment to see one another later today, and I'm confident we won't be troubling the Court with any argument on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You will recall the issue that Mr. Ostojic and I were dealing with, with the United States and the aerial imagery. And I think we are very close to solving that problem as well, but I will, of course, need Mr. Ostojic here. And there is one more item that we had promised them that will come in the next day or so, but we are very close to resolving that. So we haven't forgotten about that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as the other witness scheduled for this week, yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Since we have got a moment. I liaised with Mr. Thayer at the last break, and I appreciate that he's not in court at the moment. He's provided me with a courtesy bundle of the memoranda documents. That I'm going to look at overnight and report back to him. As far as the sit-reps are concerned, that will take him a little bit longer. That's a rather more time-consuming task. So jointly, in effect, I'm asking for a bit more time for him to do that. I know he's working very hard in relation to the Court's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We all are, Mr. Josse. Thank you, although self-praise is no recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It wasn't self praise, Your Honour. It was praise for my learned friend who prosecutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. McCloskey's was self-praise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was meant for everyone, and it was probably a little bit -- well, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we are satisfied a little bit with the progress, although we are pretty sure that more could be done, especially if you cut down further on your time to finish your case, Mr. McCloskey. So there being no other business to transact, I think we have to adjourn. The sitting tomorrow is in the afternoon, as you all recall, at 2.15 in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
